utterances.text: I think we're mixing up now some things. We were talking about the 10th. On the 10th the people were still in Srebrenica. They were gathering in the vicinity of the UN compound. And I think that when we're talking about this document, we're talking about the 12th or the 13th when the people already left, because they didn't want to leave. They wanted to stay on the UN compound in Srebrenica. The 11th in the morning or in the afternoon we managed to get them in a northern direction, and after that, this is the text we can use but not on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. I appreciate it. Is it correct that some people tried to prevent civilians from leaving Srebrenica and moving towards Potocari, that there were some men in uniform who were milling among the civilians and who prevented or tried to prevent the people from leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't have the impression that on the 10th there were men in uniform who tried to prevent people leaving Srebrenica. I think they decided themselves to stay where they were because, as I told you before, at one moment on the 11th we had to arrange that they went upwards towards Potocari. But on the 11th they had only one goal: Stay near their own houses or stay on the UN compound, which was a safe place for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now once again request that Ms. Stewart assist us. Video P1147, the same video-clip, V000-9265, from the eighth minute, 5 seconds, through 8 minutes, 10 seconds. So just a very brief 5-second-long video-clip. Please observe especially the bottom of the video-clip. You see the sentence there where they are trying people to stop. We see that this person in civilian clothing said: C'mon, stay. Where are you going? Addressing the mass of people. And according to this video-clip this was recorded on the 10th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: But what do you want to prove with this, that there is somebody who is telling the people: Stay here? Well, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the screen you can see a man with a Kalashnikov, a uniformed man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just replay these five seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The man moving from left to right, do you see him?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: From left to right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could you observe that on the 10th in Srebrenica there were civilians and armed soldiers and they were mingled together; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also see, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- somebody with a blue helmet having a -- three of them, but one of them definitely having something that looks like a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So I don't know the other person that you showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Near the place where this man with weapons moving around, this was in a location that was very close to the Dutch Battalion compound in Srebrenica itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And these men in blue helmets, they're members of the DutchBat; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I still was unable to identify where the man with a Kalashnikov is. Could we take it perhaps shot by shot --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that -- here we see that someone says: Come on, stay. Well, where are you going?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Forward a couple of seconds ahead. One more, one more, one more. Okay, stop. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see -- let me see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a green uniform [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is that -- are you referring to a person whose head is visible more or less on the red blouse of a lady?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have identified. Is that what you saw as well, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have -- is it a Kalashnikov? Can you identify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't identify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you identify at all that it's a fire weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to be a long rifle weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we perhaps go a few seconds back again so that I can see the sequence because now I know what to look for. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Now could we have the same video from the 13th minute, 48 seconds, through 14 minutes, 10 seconds. Can we just pause briefly at the 14th minute, 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see here -- we can hear a voice in the background but you can also see it on the transcript. It says: "Man, our army went up there." And we see some people board or are trying to get on the bus. And this is on the compound itself in Srebrenica. This is the situation where you described that the civilians had broken through the fence and moved into the compound area and tried to board these trucks; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we play the video now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But can I add something? Because I see a shot now and I think the shot is made from outside the compound point towards the compound and men of "our army went up there," that could be everywhere, not on the truck. Because I think you suggest now that men of the army went up there, that they went in the UN truck, but I think that's jumping to the conclusion because when somebody is taking --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I'm not suggesting that. It's completely different sequence. It's --

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- after that -- couple of minutes after the video we saw before. So we have to concentrate with this and I don't claim it's the same occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move it -- play it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can hear a voice speaking and we can see on the video itself: [In English] "You see our army is up there, all around." [Interpretation] This is some local person from Srebrenica speaking. Is it correct that at that point in time the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm not yet aware of who is speaking. You put that to the witness, but perhaps you could ask the witness whether he knows who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I doubt that, that he might know but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because it was obviously translated from B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and let me then just -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can play it again, if you want, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not it. But you say, are only local people from Srebrenica speaking B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. But on the -- I can clarify whether there was any Serb soldiers on the 10th in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about soldiers yet. You assume a lot of things and the basis for such assumptions is not yet clear. Whether the witness could help us, you may of course give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rave, do you know who made this video-clip and do you know who is speaking here? I assume you don't but can you please answer?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I really don't know who made it and who is speaking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, 1995, the Army of Republika Srpska was not in Srebrenica; correct? Not in this area where this video was made from?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, they still were in the southern part of the area and in the southern part in the outskirts of the town of Srebrenica, not in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many Serbs at that point in time lived in Srebrenica? Were there any Serbs living in Srebrenica other than one woman and her disabled son who were killed before this?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I've no idea that there lived any Serb in Srebrenica during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just intervene. I see Mr. Lukic asked you that: "On the 10th of July, 1995, the Army of Republika Srpska was not in Srebrenica." Are you able to see from this footage the date when this was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the date of the 11th, but as you know, on a video camera you can change dates and timings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But the fact is what we see here is the 11th, not the 10th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, as I told you on the 11th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking for your opinion. I'm saying what we see on the picture is the 11th, not the 10th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be the 11th because on the 10th there were no refugees on the compound. And we see them now on the compound, so it must be the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what about the presence of the VRS or Serbs on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 11th the VRS was in the southern part. As I told you, we had blocking positions about in the middle of the town of Srebrenica. In the southern part the Serbs were there moving northwards. So there were Serbs in Srebrenica, but not in this area because this is already the northern part of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that BH army members were not always easy to recognise because -- or to distinguish because they wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Because there was no standing army and hardly none of them wore a uniform, now and then only parts of a uniform, we knew them by person and not by military outfits or ranks or those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What knowledge, if any, do you have about members of the 28th Division of the BH army mingling with civilians who were moving -- who had set off towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have no idea if members of the BiH army were in the stream of refugees because I don't think that men in uniform went upwards to Potocari. Most of them in uniform disappeared in the evening of the 10th to the 11th in a north-western direction. I can't remember having seen people in uniform going northwards towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We established that some members of the 28th Division of the BH army did not wear uniforms. We can assume then, that if they were moving with civilians and if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- can you exclude the possibility that among the civilians that were moving towards Potocari there were also members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I can't exclude it because there were men in an age that normally they would be in the army. They were wearing civilian clothes, so there's always a possibility that there were members or former members from the BiH army among those men going upward to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you look at the transcript, you'll see that the interpreters missed one of your words. If you would read your question again and tell us what is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this part has sense. I wasn't reading so that's the question I wanted to pose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we now briefly see in e-court 18217, that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we further look at that, Witness, could you tell us the following if we saw the text that is: "You see, our army is up there and around." At the 11th of July, were there still positions held by the BiH forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, not because I think we were the only ones who had the blocking positions in the town of Srebrenica and the BiH army already were gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my opinion because I was on the compound and not outside of the compound, so I really can't confirm that they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the information you had was such that you thought they would not be there anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that the Muslim army only around 1500 hours on the 11th of July set out towards Jaglici? Was it at 1500 hours they were close to this location and around it?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: On the 11th on 1500 hours I was on the compound of the Bravo Company in Srebrenica and I really don't know if there were parts of the BiH army in that vicinity, as I just told Mr. Oric [sic]. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please take a look at this document on the screen, the one that speaks about general mobilisation. It is stated that on the basis of the order of the Presidency of the Republic of BH, general mobilisation is being declared. This is a document from 1992, and it was stated that general mobilisation is being declared of all able-bodied citizens from 16 to 60 years of age for the purpose of joining Territorial Defence units, public security stations, civilian protection units, and compulsory work service. Do you know about Srebrenica, whether general mobilisation had been declared there for all from age 16 to 60?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I can't see the date of the document. I can see the investigation date, it was 2004, but I can't the date of the document. And if it might have been in 2002, of course there's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 1992, the document is from 1992.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: 1992. Well, that was three years before the UN entered the enclave and of course it might be possible that I don't know and I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking if you are aware, not --

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you might just help me, how do we determine that the date of this document is 1992? Where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since there is no date, Your Honour, on the document but it says -- it's talking only about TO, Territorial Defence, and afterwards there was no TO that there was Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So having this TO then we know that it's from 1992 and I wasn't able to locate the date as well. That's why I wasn't claiming that it's -- the document is from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When in 1992 did the TO come to an end?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably summer 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instead of guessing, is there any shared views on when the TO ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it seems something that perhaps you could agree on as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope -- I'm sure that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- many other matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if in addition to that you could agree on a few more matters which -- then which apparently are not in dispute, it would be highly appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to deal with the Dutch Battalion in more specific terms. Is it correct that your battalion, the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica, could not ask for support from NATO aircraft unless they were attacked themselves by one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: We could, of course, ask support as many times as we would, but of course there must be reason to ask support. The decisions to provide us with air support in whatever way was on the higher levels and not even in Tuzla, but it was in Sarajevo and even in Zagreb, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, is it correct that you yourselves had to be attacked or under threat, you as a battalion? Or could you ask for support also if the VRS were to attack the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I can't answer that question correctly because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D887, could we please have a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is your testimony in the Tolimir case on the 27th of October, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 51 in e-court and it is supposed to correspond to page 6868 of the transcript in the Tolimir case. We need lines 13 through 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read this out in English. From line 13, quote: [In English] "Did soldiers and officers of the DutchBat on the ground know that without an attack by the Bosnian Serb army against UNPROFOR positions there could be no close air support, in other words, the bombing of Bosnian Serb army positions?" And your answer from line 17 was: "Yes, I think this was common knowledge, and that was also communicated by the battalion staff. We were attacked, and this was one of the things we discussed this morning before when Captain Hageman went forward to see if the VRS attack went on. He was shot at. So he got a confirmation that the UN was attacked, and that was enough for close air support."

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think we're mixing up again two things. Talking about air support in general or talking about air support in this specific case, because in this case we're referring to an ultimatum that was sent to the parties on the 10th of July and in that ultimatum was the statement that when UN positions were attacked that it would be possible for the battalion to ask for air support. So in this specific case it was clear that when the blocking positions were attacked or UN persons were attacked we were able to ask for close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question, the one that I don't think I've received an answer to yet, is the following: Could you ask for air support if the Army of Republika Srpska were to attack the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or was the prerequisite that UNPROFOR members would have to have their security and safety compromised?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had no positions because they didn't exist as an army during the period we were there. As I told you, when tensions got stronger, parts of the BiH soldiers went in the vicinity of the UN OPs and tried to get fire on the UN OPs so that when the UN OPs were attacked, they were involved, and of course there was a possibility for us to ask for air support. It was of course not the way that if there were units of the BiH, as far as you can speak about units, that we protect them with our close air support. We were there to protect the enclave, to deter attacks, and to protect ourself, and not to protect the BiH army with supporting them with close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this clarification. On the 10th of July, 1995, your forces stood before the advancing forces of the Army of Republika Srpska and they blocked the access to Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: We tried to block because we had our OPs already in the southern part of the enclave, and the VRS went forward all the time. And we had to move backwards with our OPs and we weren't able because we had no ammunition or anything else enough to deter the attack in a proper way. So -- but the only thing we could do was try to block the VRS when they attacked as much as possible and to gain as much as possible time also for the higher echelons eventually to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you first asked for air support on the 10th of July, 1995, but that you did not get it, and it was only after that that Mr. Franken issued an order to block the road where the Serb units were advancing?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: We were blocking the roads already after the fall of OP Echo in the south. We made several blocking positions or OPs, whatever you can call them, and I think that the first time when we were attacked on the 10th, that physically the VRS attacked UN positions, in my opinion - but I'm not sure because I didn't do it myself - that there was a question for close air support on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the evening, on the 10th, you had a meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Karremans. Somewhere it says "Lieutenant-Colonel" and somewhere it says "Colonel." At the time was Mr. Karremans a lieutenant-colonel? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As a battalion commander he was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the evening, did you attend a meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans with the representatives of the civilian and military authorities of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that that evening, Mr. Karremans promised the representatives of the Muslim military and civilian authorities that the Serb positions would be bombed and that that would not only be close air support; rather, there would be heavy bombing of the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. He told the civilian and the military authorities that when the attacks - as was stated in the ultimatum - was going on, the next morning there would be a possibility for an air-strike, so a heavy bombing of a part in the terrain, and possibility for close air support.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can hardly hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have some noise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters have difficulties hearing you. There is something technically -- there is a kind of echo on the line. And since I don't like to hear myself again -- yes, and it changed halfway, then it went back to a different level. Are there any ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we check microphones on the accused bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, apparently there isn't. I still hear a kind of a rumble, a kind of -- could everyone switch his microphone off to see whether that sound remains. When I just opened my microphone, nothing special happens. Could the microphone of the witness be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the microphone of the witness be replaced by another one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your microphone is still on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Problem solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. It's fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this same time, did your battalion receive orders to open fire at Serb units? I'm not asking about you personally but the battalion as a whole.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because I was not in that line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at what Mr. Franken said at the Tolimir trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D885 is what we need. That's the trial transcript, page 71. It should correspond to transcript page 3473 in the Tolimir trial. From line 5 up to line 10, that's what we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Question, [In English] I quote: "Tell me, when did you issue the green order? "A. That must have been the evening of the 9th of July. "Q. ... does that mean that, from then on, your soldiers have no restrictions with respect to the use of the weapons that they had at their disposal? "A. That's correct." [Interpretation] Do you know that on the 9th of July, 1995, Mr. Franken issued the green order? And can you tell us what the green order is?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Franken gave a green order. It might have been on the 9th, that might be possible, but because I was not in a fighting unit but always in the negotiation position, I didn't even read this order because it was more for the both companies, Charlie and the Bravo Companies, that were to deal with this and, of course, the battalion staff on the compound in the operation room. But I didn't read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what a green order is, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness also explain to us what his understanding of a green order is because you asked him and you may be interested in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am, I just repeated it, but you were talking with Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A green order is not a common word in the communications, but in this case, I would say that all the orders we used as UNPROFOR were blue orders and we acted as UNPROFOR. In my opinion, this green order does only mean that we stop being visible, being only deterring attacks, but going into a real war situation and firing against the enemy that attacks us and more in a green way than in a blue way. Because in an UNPROFOR situation, I don't think that we were able to go in really fighting a war. And when you want to go into the situation that you act as real soldiers, then you have to go -- to do it in a green way. It's a little bit difficult for me to explain what the real difference is between green and blue because the green order doesn't exist. It's just an order. And we switched a little bit more from blue towards green, and I think that's why it was called a green order. Because normally, as you know, the positions we were on, in an OP, for example, was on the top of the hill with a lot of light, white vehicles, white markings on everything, so that's not a military position. That's a sitting duck who is looking around. And when you have to fight a war and defend yourself, then you go in another mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, the platoon that you were in. We have some documents here too, but this is what I'm going to ask you. Would you agree with me that you did know at that point in time that your battalion was actually in a combat position and that it actually started firing at the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a few questions together. Could you split up, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know, did anyone inform you, did Mr. Franken inform you that the position of your battalion in the Srebrenica enclave had been changed and that the rules of using the weapons that you had available were changed too?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have to answer the question in yes and no. I know that our role changed, but I also know that in -- as far as I remember, the order was not directly to fire on the VRS soldiers, but to fire overhead. Because we were in the minority, we had no possibilities to go into a real fight, so the only thing was to try to deter, warn them, and give them the warning by firing overhead that they had to stop. And I don't think that there was an order, as far as I know, directly to attack the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek some clarification there as well. Part of your answer suggests - that's at least what I hear - that it was firing -- returning fire if they would not stop, unless I misunderstood that. Whereas at the end you say -- that there was no -- I don't think there was an order directly to attack the VRS. Now, we have two issues apparently. The one is whether or not to fire and the second is whether or not to attack or to return an attack. Could you, in your answer, distinguish between these two elements of what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you are directly personally attacked, either on person or in a vehicle, then you have the possibility to try to stop the attack on those vehicles, on those persons. When an attack is going on from front -- from the enemy, as we call it from this moment on, I think, we were not able to stop them because we hadn't the vehicles, we hadn't the ammunition, we hadn't the weapons to stop them, so the order was to try to deter the attack by firing overhead, warning them, and warning them by stopping. The other possibility was, of course, and that was in the other stage, that we asked for close air support. The UN was attacked, we didn't have the means ourselves to defend ourselves enough, so we asked for close air support and then we got a direct attack on the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there -- were you allowed in any way to fire at whomever without you being fired at before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, before that it wasn't possible because only when you were attacked yourself or somebody else and you had to stop it, then you were able to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see that order?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I didn't see the green order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct that Mr. Franken knew better what kind of order he had issued?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, because he was the one who organised the operational part of the whole party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue shortly, but we have to take the break now because this is our time for the regular break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break, but could we first invite the witness to leave the courtroom. We resume in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes from now means 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, could you give us an indication as to where we are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see that I have a lot. I think that I can finish maybe a bit before the time I asked for since this witness for us is very important to explain some crucial things from those crucial days in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and again your estimate was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five hours. And you think you could -- okay. Then we'll -- but you say there's even a little chance that you would finish earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were discussing what sort of order Mr. Franken had issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to look at 1D885. I think that we have the document on our screens. We need page 51 in the e-court, which should correspond to page 3453. That's the transcript page from the Tolimir case. We need lines 12 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will be reading a larger portion. [In English] "Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, did the green order mean that an engagement in combat operations should be undertaken regardless of what was contained in blue, red, and other orders? "A. I do not know whether I understand your question correctly, but it meant that, for instance, the rules of engagement given to us before as a UN unit, one of our problems we were only to use our weapons in self-defence, were ruled out and we went back to the rules of engagement of an army, any army, in combat. "Q. Thank you for clarifying this. Can you tell us now, please, were you already a legitimate target of those whose lives you threatened through these combat operations, as you described them? "A. As of the issuing of the green order, we were in combat with the VRS, and the VRS was a target for us, and in fact the opposite is realistic and true as well." [Interpretation] Do you agree that Mr. Franken had -- was in a better position to be informed of the situation and have a better assessment of what the situation was like after the green order was issued? And I'm referring to the situation that the DutchBat found itself in after the order was issued.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think the order was issued by Mr. Franken himself, so I think he took the decision together with Colonel Karremans to issue this order. And in a better position, well, I think that they took the decision to protect their own unit and, as much as possible, the people of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to read something from page 81 of the same document which should correspond to -- that's page 81 in e-court. It should correspond to page number 3483 of the transcript from the Tolimir case, where General Tolimir asked Mr. Franken from line 22 through to the end of the page and we have to move on to the next page up until line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you what I will base my question on. Line 22: [In English] "Q. And was it within your mandate to destroy the weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska and to go to war with the VRS after the green order had been issued ...? "A. No, not within the mandate, but then again, my mandate was" - and we have to go to another page, and I quote again - "changed significantly the very moment the UN ordered me to defend Srebrenica, and that was the cause why I gave that green order in that sequence it was. So there's a period of mandate being till the order of the UN to my battalion to defend the city, and after that, the rules of engagement, et cetera, all restrictions on the use of weapons, were gone because that goes with the order to defend something. I can't defend something by sweetly talking with everybody and standing -- just standing there. I had to use and was authorised to use my weapons." [Interpretation] Would you agree with me that the DutchBat, after the order was issued, and I mean the green order, was at war with the Army of Republika Srpska and that VRS members were a target for the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think that you state now that we were in a war, yes, we were in a war because we were attacked as being in a war, and I think we tried to defend ourselves and the population of the enclave with all the means we had - and that wasn't too much. But of course you get a situation that you can speak of a war situation, but it was not declaring a war towards anybody. We just got into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we are talking about apparently two orders, one order by the UN that the mandate was changed and a green order. We are talking about it. I haven't seen any order. Is there any recording, written or otherwise, of the one order, the UN order, as the witness told us, or the order issued by Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All I located by now was this testimony of Mr. Franken and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, Mr. Stojanovic, who was part of two Srebrenica trials told -- just told me that he has never seen any written order in this regard. Maybe that can be found somewhere in -- among US cables -- UN cables, but we haven't located it yet. We'll try to locate those orders as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because if I -- if I understand what Mr. Franken apparently has said - you quoted that - they were just in an ordinary combat situation, which would mean that you would take territory -- I mean, is that all involved? I've got no idea but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have Mr. Franken in a couple of days here in front of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then we'll see what he tells us. Were you ever informed about the green order and what it exactly was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know about the existence of the green order and I know that we went into a kind of war situation, but I've never seen the order and I've never seen exactly what was in it and what would be my role in it. My mandate didn't change because we just went on with our work. The only thing I think is the most important thing for the two companies who had to do the operational part of the things, they got the green order. And I think that the rest of the battalion just went on as we did before the green order was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you've explained to us that, first of all, that there's not the green order but there was an order you called the green order of which you do not know the content exactly. Second, that one of the consequences was to going more in a military situation, green -- more the direction of green rather than blue, that you would be less visible and that you would fire if there was any fire at you, either if you identified the source of fire clearly that you would fire at that target and, otherwise, if it was a broader kind of an attack that you would fire --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Overhead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- overhead. To your knowledge, was there anything else in that order you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really don't know what else was in that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the discussions began to reach an agreement whereby the DutchBat would side with the BH army in the fighting against the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: There wasn't a real agreement against -- between the BiH and the Dutch Battalion in fighting against the VRS. I know I was in a meeting where Mr. Franken explained to the BiH leaders in the enclave that we were sitting on the OPs, we would defend the OPs and try to deter as much as possible attacks from the VRS towards the enclave. Of course, they were aware where our OPs were and in what space there was no defence for the enclave at all. So it wasn't said loudly, but they knew we were on the OPs. They knew that there was a part of terrain between several OPs that was not defended and, of course, they could take their own plans to go into those gaps. They asked us several times that if we would leave the OPs because we were attacked, just to inform them in time so that they could take over the OPs. And of course that started already when the OP Echo fell, they wanted -- the BH wanted to go forward and take over the OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 1D888 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask the following: You said they requested that they would be informed if you would leave your OPs. Did you do it? Did you agree that you would inform them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we would not leave the OPs abandoned. It just happened when we were attacked and then left the OPs, but we didn't inform them that we left the OPs. But there were so many people in and around the OPs that they knew and they saw that we went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see here a document issued by the command of the 28th Division of the Srebrenica land forces. The document was sent by Naser Oric and we'll see that on the next page. Can we have that? We'll see that he signed as commander brigadier and it's addressed to the Chief of Staff Major Ramiz Becirovic. The letter was sent on the 31st of May, 1995. And under 1 - this is page 2 - we see that -- of course, since it's in the form of a telegram there is no handwritten signature. We need page 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And please focus on item number 1 where Naser Oric writes to Ramiz Becirovic, the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division: "You have to --" I quote: "You have to create a situation, a test for the Dutch, to see if they are genuinely prepared to shoot at the Chetniks alongside us." This was the reason why I asked you whether you knew when negotiations began between the DutchBat and representatives of the commanders of the 28th Division to the effect that members of the DutchBat would, together with members of the BH army, start fighting the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: But what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I did put my question, though it was quite long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've explained why you put an earlier question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, because I didn't get the answer on that part of my question so that's why I have to -- why I had to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you suggest now that on the 26th of May we started to negotiate with the command of the 28th Division. We started to talk to the military component in the enclave in the beginning of January when we entered. And during this whole period, of course, they tried to get advantage of us, to get their own freedom of movement, to steer us in the direction they wanted. A good example is, for example, the OP Bravo in the western part of the enclave, they wanted to decide where we would put our OP. We didn't. And of course I think the game they are talking about here was going on from the beginning of January till the end, trying to get advantage from the battalion, trying to get, it's possible, of course, as much information about the VRS, what was going on, about what was going on outside the enclave, and about how the UN would react on eventual attacks from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to discuss the night between the 10th and the 11th of July of 1995. During that night, a meeting was held between the commanders of the DutchBat and the military and civilian authorities in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the representatives of the Muslim authorities in Srebrenica were promised by Colonel Karremans that should the Serbs continue to advance towards Srebrenica, a mass-scale bombing would ensue, bombing of the Serbian positions naturally?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think I already answered the question. There was an ultimatum and the ultimatum was that when the VRS continued attacking UN positions, that there was a possibility for close air support and an air-strike. And an air-strike does mean an airship with lots of weapons on board who is able to destroy a square kilometre in the terrain. That was told that was in the ultimatum. And it was promised that when the VRS continues attacking Srebrenica and the UN, it would be asked to use those means. And then I jump directly to the answer. We asked for it the next morning when the VRS continued the attack, but we didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did I have to repeat the question? Do you know that this was also part of the changed mandate of the United Nations in Srebrenica? We had occasion to hear what Mr. Franken said, that one of the changes was basically placing the DutchBat into combat mode, that's to say, combat against personnel and assets. But what I'm asking you is: Are you aware of the fact that, generally speaking, the UN mandate changed in the sense that not just close air support would be requested but rather mass-scale bombing of the Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the change of a mandate and any mass-scale bombing, is the mass-scale bombing not part of the mandate for the units the witness belonged to or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking if he knows about the change of the mandate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because I think that before they only could ask for close air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a mandate is, from my understanding, is the task given and the means given to perform that task. That's my understanding of what a mandate is. Now, bombing is, as far as I can see, you need airplanes for that, and as far as I'm aware of, at least the units there, DutchBat did not have such means. So therefore I'm a bit confused about the change of the mandate. Do you mean the overall UNPROFOR mandate? Do you mean the specific mandate for DutchBat? And how do you link that to bombings? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How I do understand it is that before NATO could be ordered only to bomb in the immediate vicinity of the confrontation between UNPROFOR and VRS positions, obviously, since we heard before that it was never considered to bomb Muslim positions. Now the mandate was changed that you can bomb not only there but also in another parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked him if he knows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he knows about the change of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are talking about the mandate of the totality of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the forces. Okay. Let's -- let that be clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But of course I limit it only in regard to Srebrenica if the gentleman knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The general change in regard of Srebrenica. Probably he does not know anything about Bihac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem is the following, Mr. Lukic. If you are talking about the mandate and you link that to bombing, then I would expect someone to have planes to bomb. As far as I've heard, DutchBat had no planes available, which means what mandate are you talking about, the mandate of DutchBat or the UNPROFOR mandate for the whole of the territory or the UNPROFOR mandate specifically for Srebrenica? I'm just wondering what exactly it is that you want to know from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to know from him if he heard about general change of the UN mandate that affected DutchBat on the ground in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of any general change in the UN mandate which had an effect on your functioning, the functioning of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any change of the mandate. I'm only aware of orders in the chain of command as to -- although stated in the document that Mr. Franken said that he got the order, whatever it might be, to defend Srebrenica. I've never seen this order, and I didn't hear that there was a change in the mandate, not even that we went from UN over to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you had to ask for the aerial support from NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, we had to ask -- we were not NATO troops. We had to ask close air support in the UN line and, for me, the UN line ended in either Tuzla or Sarajevo. But I think that the decision for close air support was made in Zagreb and maybe not even in Zagreb. It might be even in New York. So we asked in the UN line for the support and not in the NATO line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. But you don't know how it functioned actually?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we are with this topic and we might go back to it, General Mladic accused Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans of having sought air-strikes. Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans told him, first of all, that he wasn't the one who could make such a decision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's right. He had to demand and to ask for close air support or air-strikes. He couldn't make the decision. He could just ask for it and tell his higher level that what that was in the ultimatum was violated. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that step had to be taken? NATO aircraft would not proceed to bomb unless there was one such request coming from the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: When there is in the ultimatum that we have to prove that the VRS is still attacking the UN, we send forward on the ground an APC and an APC is attacked by a VRS tank, then we got enough proof to send it up in the line, and they have to decide either we get close air support or air-strikes or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the ultimatum has been mentioned several times. Could we inquire with the witness whether that ultimatum is formalised anywhere, whether it's recorded anywhere, so that we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Witness, you could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen the ultimatum nor the green order so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say, "I have not seen the ultimatum."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where and when and by whom was that ultimatum made, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Colonel Karremans made me aware of the ultimatum and talked about the ultimatum and explained it to the Muslim military and civilian leaders in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only -- that's the only thing I'm aware of of the ultimatum, and he explained that in the ultimatum was what I've just told you. But I've never seen a written ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that ultimatum was addressed to the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "also." To whom was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was to the Bosnian Serb forces and it was explained to the Muslims in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it an oral ultimatum? Was it made orally or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a written ultimatum and I may find it in my notes when it was brought to, I think, the OP Papa to hand it over in the VRS line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking to the parties whether there's any awareness of a written document which contains the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to check my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I'm not. It's never been really contested, but we can double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the ultimatum not contested or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, it's never been contested. It's clearly part of the history of this case and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, the reason why I'm asking for it because I'd like to know what it exactly says. If it's put on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we can take a look. The higher-ranking officers that are more involved in this have a clearer recollection, as has been referred to already, but we'll take a good look for documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, at the same time I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Rave, we'll adjourn for the day and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the same courtroom. But before you leave, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, and irrespective of whether that's testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 24th of April, Courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of April, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
